content.title: Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems
content.overview: This lesson covers two fundamental existence theorems in calculus: the Extreme Value Theorem (EVT) and the Mean Value Theorem (MVT). These theorems provide guarantees about the behavior of functions on closed intervals, provided specific conditions of continuity and differentiability are met.
learning_objectives: Verify the hypotheses of the Extreme Value Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem.
Apply the Extreme Value Theorem to find absolute extrema on a closed interval.
Apply the Mean Value Theorem to find values of c where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change.
Distinguish between existence and uniqueness in the context of these theorems.

sections.title: The Extreme Value Theorem (EVT)
sections.content: The Extreme Value Theorem states that if a function f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], then f must attain an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum value on that interval. The 'Candidates Test' is the standard procedure for finding these values: you must evaluate the function at all critical points (where f'(x) = 0 or is undefined) located within the interval (a, b) and at the two endpoints, a and b. The largest resulting value is the absolute maximum, and the smallest is the absolute minimum.

sections.title: The Mean Value Theorem (MVT)
sections.content: The Mean Value Theorem connects the average rate of change over an interval to the instantaneous rate of change at a point within that interval. For MVT to apply, two conditions must be met: 1) f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b], and 2) f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b). If these hold, there exists at least one number c in the open interval (a, b) such that f'(c) = [f(b) - f(a)] / [b - a]. Geometrically, this means there is at least one point where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line passing through the endpoints.

sections.title: Hypotheses-Then-Compute Strategy
sections.content:
Before applying these theorems, you must explicitly confirm their hypotheses. For EVT, check only for continuity on [a, b]. For MVT, you must check both continuity on [a, b] and differentiability on (a, b). If a function has a sharp turn (like an absolute value) or a vertical tangent within the interval, it is not differentiable there, and MVT cannot be guaranteed. Once hypotheses are confirmed, compute the target: for MVT, calculate the average rate of change; for EVT, identify critical points.

![A flow chart showing the steps to apply the Mean Value Theorem: Verify continuity on a,b, Verify differentiability on (a,b), Calculate average rate of change, Set f prime of c equal to average rate, Solve for c in (a,b).](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/a952d4ba-04bc-422e-be0a-0eff159e8365-1786519357802-893.webp)

worked_examples.question: Let f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 5 on the interval [-2, 2]. Find all values of c guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Check hypotheses. f(x) is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [-2, 2] and differentiable on (-2, 2). MVT applies.
Step 2: Calculate the average rate of change. f(2) = (2)^3 - 3(2) + 5 = 8 - 6 + 5 = 7. f(-2) = (-2)^3 - 3(-2) + 5 = -8 + 6 + 5 = 3. Average rate = (7 - 3) / (2 - (-2)) = 4 / 4 = 1.
Step 3: Find f'(x). f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3.
Step 4: Set f'(c) equal to the average rate. 3c^2 - 3 = 1 => 3c^2 = 4 => c^2 = 4/3 => c = ±√(4/3) or ±2/√3.
Step 5: Verify c is in the open interval (-2, 2). Both ±2/√3 (approx ±1.15) are within (-2, 2). Thus, c = 2/√3 and c = -2/√3.

common_mistakes: Applying MVT to a function that is not differentiable at a point inside the interval (e.g., f(x) = |x| on [-1, 1]).
Forgetting to check the endpoints when looking for absolute extrema using EVT.
Assuming MVT guarantees only one value of c; it guarantees at least one, but there could be many.
Confusing the average rate of change (slope of secant) with the average value of the function (integral-based).
exam_tips: Always state 'Since f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)...' before invoking MVT to earn full justification points.
If a question asks if a specific value of the derivative must exist, look for the average rate of change first.
For EVT, the 'absolute maximum' refers to the y-value, while the 'location' refers to the x-value.
Remember that differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability.
content.recap: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees absolute extrema on a closed interval for continuous functions. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change, provided the function is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open interval.

knowledge_claims.content: The Extreme Value Theorem (EVT) guarantees that a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] will have both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum value.
To apply the Mean Value Theorem (MVT), a function must be continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and differentiable on the open interval (a, b).
The Mean Value Theorem states there exists at least one c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a).
The Candidates Test for absolute extrema involves evaluating the function at all critical points in the open interval and at both endpoints of the closed interval.
Geometrically, the Mean Value Theorem guarantees the existence of a tangent line that is parallel to the secant line connecting the endpoints of the interval.
It is a mistake to apply the Mean Value Theorem if the function has a cusp, corner, or vertical tangent (non-differentiability) anywhere within the open interval (a, b).
While EVT only requires continuity on the closed interval, MVT requires both continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval.
If a problem asks to prove that a particle's instantaneous velocity was equal to its average velocity at some point, the Mean Value Theorem is the appropriate tool.
When solving for c in the MVT, one must verify that the resulting c-values actually lie within the open interval (a, b); values at the endpoints do not satisfy the theorem's conclusion.
The Mean Value Theorem guarantees the existence of at least one value c, but it does not guarantee that the value is unique.
If f'(x) > 0 for all x in an interval, the Mean Value Theorem can be used to prove that the function is strictly increasing on that interval.
A critical point of a function f is a value x in the domain where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) is undefined.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems: Theorems guarantee extrema or a derivative equal to an average rate only when their continuity and differentiability hypotheses are satisfied.
options.B: Numerical Integration and Error Direction: Trapezoidal and midpoint approximations use tabular data, and concavity or monotonicity can determine likely over- or underestimation.
options.C: Logistic Differential Equations: Logistic growth includes a carrying capacity, has maximum growth at half that capacity, and approaches equilibrium rather than increasing without bound.
options.D: Vector-Valued Motion: Differentiating a position vector gives velocity, speed is the magnitude of velocity, and acceleration is the velocity derivative.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Theorems guarantee extrema or a derivative equal to an average rate only when their continuity and differentiability hypotheses are satisfied. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.
options.B: Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems: Theorems guarantee extrema or a derivative equal to an average rate only when their continuity and differentiability hypotheses are satisfied.
options.C: Average Value and Net Change: The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved.
options.D: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves: Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives.

videoLesson.title: Verify Conditions to Apply MVT and EVT
videoLesson.description: Confirm continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval, then compute the required values. Include endpoints for extremes and use interior points for mean value conclusions.
